claims.text: Low hardness and strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi arise from a low density of impediments to dislocation motion in its homogeneous solid-solution state.
Lattice distortion in the CoCrFeNiTi solid solution is only moderate.
The simple solid-solution state lacks second-phase particles and other significant microstructural obstacles.
The scarcity of obstacles permits easy dislocation motion and produces a low critical resolved shear stress.
Easy dislocation motion results in limited strain hardening while retaining good ductility.
The proposed initial material is fully annealed, homogeneous, single-phase, and coarse-grained.
Aging or mechanical processing can be used to introduce nanoscale precipitates, grain refinement, or both into the comparison samples.
Nanoscale precipitates and refined grain boundaries act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
The control and modified samples are intended to have identical overall CoCrFeNiTi compositions.
The density and distribution of precipitates and grain boundaries govern dislocation interactions, multiplication, and strain hardening.
Lattice distortion in the simple CoCrFeNiTi solid solution is insufficient to provide significant solid-solution strengthening.
The absence of precipitates and refined grains causes early plastic flow and low hardness and yield strength.
The as-solid-solution state will have lower yield strength and hardness than samples containing nanoscale precipitates or refined grains.
Deformation of the as-solid-solution state will be dominated by relatively smooth dislocation glide.
TEM of the as-solid-solution state will reveal few dislocation obstacles or secondary phases.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state combines favorable plasticity and machinability with relatively low hardness and strength.
The proposed mechanism is asserted to apply under quasi-static loading from room temperature to approximately 600 °C, provided recovery or dynamic recrystallization does not dominate.

Failure of introduced precipitates or grain refinement to measurably increase hardness and yield strength, together with similar dislocation behavior in both sets, would falsify the obstacle-scarcity hypothesis.
